blocks.en: ReLEAF’s hardware centers on a closed-loop hollow-fiber bioreactor designed to bring protectant production closer to the farm, reducing the transport, storage, and repeated purchasing associated with externally manufactured products. To make on-site production practical, the system combines a 0.2 µm hollow-fiber module with circulation pumps, pressure and flow monitoring, in-line OD600 measurement, and controlled recovery from the shell side. Across three integrated runs, the bioreactor supported continuous culture, real-time monitoring, extracellular ACC deaminase recovery, and whole-cell retention, with no colonies observed from plated shell-side samples under the tested conditions. We also developed an assembly guide and user manual to make the hardware easier to reproduce and adapt for future on-site biomanufacturing systems.

2.1 從 TgPGPR 到一部生物反應器

blocks.en: Climate change makes crop stress more frequent and harder to predict, and we want to give crops a genetically modified bioprotectant to help them cope. Our first design was a transgenic plant‑growth‑promoting rhizobacterium (TgPGPR) that would live on the roots and make the protectant there.
blocks.text: Climate change makes crop stress more frequent and harder to predict, and we want to give crops a genetically modified bioprotectant to help them cope. Our first design was a transgenic plant‑growth‑promoting rhizobacterium (TgPGPR) that would live on the roots and make the protectant there.
blocks.zh: 氣候變遷讓作物逆境更頻繁、也更難預測，我們想給作物一種基因改造的生物保護劑，幫牠們應付。我們最初的設計是一株轉基因的植物生長促進根圈細菌（TgPGPR），讓牠住在根上、就地製造保護劑。

blocks.en: We chose a bioreactor instead, for two reasons. The main one is biosafety. Once a transgenic organism is released, its expression, dose and spread can no longer be controlled. The other is survival. Lab strains of Bacillus subtilis lack motility, can’t form biofilm and have metabolic deficiencies, so they would struggle in the field anyway.

blocks.en: We only need the protectant in the field, so we keep the organism in a machine and send out only its product. That turns a release problem into a containment problem.

blocks.zh: 2.2 為何選用 Bacillus subtilis 與灌流式中空纖維

blocks.en: We chose Bacillus subtilis because the FDA classifies nonpathogenic, nontoxigenic strains as Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) under good manufacturing practices. It is easy to engineer, and it secretes recombinant protein into the medium, so the cells never have to be broken open to collect the protectant.
blocks.text: We chose Bacillus subtilis because the FDA classifies nonpathogenic, nontoxigenic strains as Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) under good manufacturing practices. It is easy to engineer, and it secretes recombinant protein into the medium, so the cells never have to be broken open to collect the protectant.
blocks.zh: 我們選用 Bacillus subtilis，因為 FDA 把非病原、非產毒的菌株在良好製造規範下列為一般認為安全（GRAS）。它容易進行工程改造，而且會把重組蛋白質分泌到培養基中，因此不必破開細胞就能收取保護劑。

blocks.en: We used two strains. B. subtilis 168 ran the growth tests and the first integrated run, where it barely made detectable enzyme, probably because its own secreted proteases broke the product down. Every later run used B. subtilis WB800, which lacks those proteases (4.2, prototype 1). Both are nonpathogenic lab strains, and the hardware is the same for either.

blocks.en: A second growth after the plateau is not what a batch curve does. Our working explanation is that the erythromycin degraded, the cells began to lose the plasmid, and with less metabolic burden they grew again. Plasmid stability was what Prof. Chang asked about in September (6.1). Strain 168 also barely made detectable ACC deaminase, probably because its secreted proteases degrade the product, so the next prototype uses B. subtilis WB800, which lacks them. The unstable pressure readings still need explaining; the electronics review that followed is in 6.2.

blocks.en: We also worked out how to sterilize the assembled loop without an autoclave, by chemical clean‑in‑place (CIP). We pump in 900 mL of distilled water, then 100 mL of 35% hydrogen peroxide; they mix in the lumen reservoir and circulate for 15 minutes, and a starch–iodide test paper checks for peroxide. The solution drains through a tube, which is reattached to close the loop. Then 1 L of distilled water circulates for 30 minutes, with a fresh test paper after each wash, until no peroxide is left. It usually takes five 1 L washes.

blocks.en: The run started on October 14, 2026. Since prototype 2 had shown both sides read the same (its Learn), protectant was drawn from the shell side only, twice, at hours 1.10 and 18.38. At the 38‑hour mark, unnoticed at the time, a Luer valve at the start of the lumen loop broke in half and medium leaked into the incubator. Up to then the pH and OD curves were reliable: clear readings of growth, and of how the pH responded to growth and to KOH. The OD rose from 0.14 to 2.71 by 37 h, a fitted growth rate of 0.286 h−1 (notebook, week 33). That is inside the range forecast before the run. After 38 hours the pump’s shaking had knocked the photometer’s light path out of line, so later OD data cannot be used.

blocks.en: Prototype 3 called for the pH to be corrected automatically (its Learn), so this cycle automates both the pH control and the shell‑side sampling. With help from Owl Lab, we built a valve controller driven by an STS3215 serial bus servo. This Luer valve controller works together with the pinch valve, which is driven by the same type of servo. blocks.en: Two things changed in the bioreactor. The first is the pair of servo‑driven valves, the pinch valve and the Luer valve controller. They let us sample the shell permeate and record the pressure change at the same time, and the pressure transducer readings show whether the pinch valve drives the product from the lumen medium into the shell permeate.

blocks.en: Against DBTL 2 (5.1), this run follows the shell side nearly twice as long, through 72 h instead of 40 h, at a similar level: the ELISA peak of 6.5 µg/mL at 12 h compares with 7.2 µg/mL near 16 h then (time course), and the activity is now given in units. blocks.en: Servo controlWe had planned a PCA9685 driver board for the servos that turn the Luer valve and the pinch valve. In his experience it is unreliable. Told to turn 90°, it may stop at 85°, and a valve that misses its position can cause a sudden pressure spike that breaks the tubing and leaks. The servos also lacked the torque to turn the valves. He suggested the STS3215 servo, driven over UART, which is accurate and strong enough.

blocks.en: Control boardThe Arduino UNO Q uses 3.3 V logic, not the usual 5 V, so the pumps, motors and sensors need their voltage stepped. blocks.en: MainboardTwo boards would have meant a bulky package with wires everywhere. Instead, one mainboard contains everything: a converter from 12 V to 5 V and 3.3 V, and every UNO Q pin brought onto it, so the board in effect becomes the UNO Q. It supplies the current the AMS1117 could not, and it keeps the 3.3 V UNO Q apart from the pumps and valves, the aim of the two‑board plan. blocks.en: The lab bioreactor already reads pressure at three membrane ports (feed, retentate and permeate) and shows the transmembrane pressure (TMP) on the dashboard (4.2); the commercial design reads all four (In‑Lumen, Out‑Lumen, In‑Shell, Out‑Shell). Today these numbers are only displayed. We will program the controller to act on them: when the lumen pressure or the TMP passes a set threshold, it sounds an alarm, stops the culture pump and opens the pinch valve.

blocks.en: Too much pressure is the condition most likely to force cells through a damaged fiber or burst a fitting, so this layer acts before a breach happens. A sudden drop can mean the membrane has already given way, often before any liquid shows, so the run stops and a shell‑side sample is plated to check (8).

blocks.en: Over a season a farmer has to top up both the medium and the culture, and neither is safe to do by hand. So the commercial bioreactor takes two sealed, single‑use cartridges: ready‑to‑use sterile medium, and a B. subtilis spore stock that ships at room temperature. Both drop into one keyed dock: the medium cartridge has a D‑shaped collar and the spore cartridge a round one, so neither fits the other’s port.

Percent B over B0 against concentration in micrograms per millilitre on a log scale: six standards from about 0.1 to 3 micrograms per millilitre on a falling fitted line, and the samples continuing the line from about 2.5 to 10 micrograms per millilitre

Three dark dashboard plots over 42 hours from 14 October 10:56. Feed flow holds near 300 to 330 mL/min, with one drop to zero at the seam

Diagram of the fourth and final integrated bioreactor. The culture bottle with B. subtilis sits on a magnetic stirrer, with a pH probe and a filter in its cap. A pump sends the culture through a flow meter, the inline photometer and a pressure transducer into the bottom of the hollow fiber membrane, out of its top past a second pressure transducer, through the pinch valve, and back through the feeding Luer valve, where a second pump adds KOH or an external feed. On the shell side a pressure transducer and the shell Luer valve lead the protectant to a separate bottle with an output line

3D model of the lab bioreactor. Drag, or use the arrow keys, to turn it; tap a part to name it.

The lab bioreactor, three-quarter view from the front left: a black wire-grid panel on two L-bracket feet, the electronics plate at the top left, the photometer on its tilted bracket, the membrane standing as a column in the middle, the culture bottle on its stirrer and the protectant bottle on a black shelf.

The controller board's component side. Top left, the power corner: a DC jack into the buck converter, a 3-digit voltmeter display, a toggle switch with a blue trimmer, and two 2-pin sockets for 12 V and ground. Female headers for the Arduino UNO Q run down both sides of the opening it sits under. Six 3-pin sensor ports, A0 to A5, run down the left edge; six, D13 to D8, down the right; eight, RX0, TX1 and D2 to D7, along the bottom; a 3-pin UART port for valve control sits bottom right; three I2C connectors for the photometer's light sensors sit top right. Each port is a 3-pin socket beside a two-row header in red, yellow and white for plus, signal and ground. Thin yellow wires join each Arduino pin to the port of the same name, thick yellow links join the ports' plus pins, and black jumper caps sit on some headers.

The solder side, seen from below so left and right swap: the Arduino header pins, each digital and analog pin with a short yellow link into the board; two bare buses beside the digital header, one from its ground pin; tinned rails under the bottom row of ports; the ports' header pins bridged in pairs; an SS34 Schottky diode by the power corner with black, red and blue leads; a white wire round the edge; a 2 by 5 and a 2 by 3 female socket
The sensor adapter cable, four views

The adapter board sealed in clear hot glue, seen from its component side: a white three-pin socket on the left marked 4 in blue, a three-pin male header on the right, both with their pins hand-marked minus, plus and S, and a round red capacitor over a blue resistor in the middle

The adapter's component side, drawn: a three by eight hole board, the socket's pins in column 2 and the header's in column 7, in rows minus, plus and S. The 15 kilo-ohm resistor lies in the S row and the 22 kilo-ohm in the plus row, between columns 3 and 6, under the 104 capacitor, whose two leads go into the minus row at columns 3 and 6

The adapter's solder side, seen from below with the S row at the top: a red wire carries plus from column 2 to 7 and a black wire carries minus round the board edge; column 3 is soldered together from the socket’s S pin as the divided output, and column 6 of the plus and minus rows with the header’s minus pin as ground; a dashed line marks the link from the 15 kilo-ohm to the header’s S, which is not marked

The adapter's circuit: plus and minus pass straight through; S comes in on the header and through 15 kilo-ohms to the socket’s S, with 22 kilo-ohms and a 0.1 microfarad capacitor from S out to ground, so 5 volts in gives about 2.97 volts out
